extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and researchers of stand-up comedy
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia-style biographical entry describing the life, career, stage persona, and public reception of a British stand-up comedian (Ian Cognito). Useful for learning what aspects of a comic's work and reputation are notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive stage persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognito had an aggressive stage persona and a reputation as Britain’s 'most banned' comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page gives concrete examples of this persona (e.g., bringing a hammer on stage, banging a nail into a wall, hanging up his hat, throwing a television from a hotel window). These actions signalled 'I really don't give a shit' and were part of his onstage identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masterful stagecraft and comic timing
rubrics_metrics.description: He was widely rated as a masterful performer with an innate grasp of stagecraft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support from tributes and commentary (comparisons to major iconoclasts; praise from peers and family). The article notes his skill as a compere and his son's and others' remarks about his timing, including anecdotes that show timing even at the moment of his death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushing the envelope / deliberate shock
rubrics_metrics.description: He described himself: 'I was always pushing the envelope. I regret the dangerous ones and tried not to be too shocking (because that is easy to do). If I did shock, there was always a reason for what I did...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames shock as a deliberate tool used with intent and occasional regret; guidance implies that shock should have a purpose and that dangerous stunts can be regrettable or risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of props and physicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of physical props and actions on stage (hammer, nails, hat; anecdote of throwing a television).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prop-driven acts were integral to his persona and performance style, serving as visual statements about his character; such physicality can define a performer's identity but carries practical and safety considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocation and controversy (banned status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation as Britain's 'most banned' comic and a history of stepping over the line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes promoters 'could no longer plead ignorance' and that he sometimes stepped over the line during or after shows — suggesting that provocation can create notoriety, affect bookings, and be part of a career trade-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autobiography and self-presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Published an autobiography, A Comedian’s Tale, which he promoted (describing it as 'the best book about comedy I have ever writ').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing memoirs or books is portrayed as part of a comedian's career and public persona; self-authored narratives contribute to legacy and public framing of one's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparisons to iconoclasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Inviting comparisons to iconoclasts like Lenny Bruce, Bill Hicks, and Jerry Sadowitz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being likened to established transgressive comedians signals a particular standard of challenging social norms and iconoclastic comedic approach; such comparisons contextualize a performer's place in comedy history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blurring performance and reality / on-stage risk
rubrics_metrics.description: His collapse onstage after joking about having a stroke was initially thought to be part of the act, illustrating how performance can blur with real-life emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the risk that highly realistic or extreme stage behavior can create for audience interpretation and performer safety; suggests awareness of how far realism should go and its potential consequences.
